The account's extra addresses (no cap but the location's free

number is kept. Lowering it releases the addresses named in
`release`, else the most recently added, a block always whole.
Buying and releasing blocks: `POST /v1/addresses`, `DELETE

When fewer addresses are paid for than the account has, the ones
to release (30-day quarantine); default the most recently added.

extra_ips.description: The account's extra addresses (no cap but the location's free space).

`pending_payment` (no active subscription yet: no address),
`active`, `suspended` (a payment is late: traffic blocked),
`canceled` (the subscription ended: traffic blocked until the
addresses are released).

accepted.description: The routes we accepted (your account's addresses, as /32s).

Your account's AS number, chosen by us: private 32-bit
(4201000000 to 4294967294), unique to your account and used by
the sessions of all its tunnels. Null until your account first
turns BGP on; it never changes after.

limit_trips.description: Times the session was closed for sending too many routes since the node's agent started.

ttl_security.description:
GTSM (ttl-security hops 1), on by default: the router
terminating the tunnel must speak BGP and send TTL 255. Off only
when your BGP speaker is one hop behind that router (we then
accept TTL 2, multihop): less protected.

announce.description: What the session may announce, as /32s (your BGP addresses and this tunnel's own).

key.description: The TCP-MD5 password or TCP-AO key (HMAC-SHA-256, key id 0 both ways); null without authentication.

your_asn.description: Your account's AS number (we chose it; the same on all your tunnels).

ttl_security.description: Keep true (the default) unless your BGP speaker is one hop behind the router terminating the tunnel; off is less protected.

TunnelConfig.description:
Everything a WireGuard client configuration needs besides its private
key. opwan routes only your static addresses (it isn't a VPN): the
dashboard's file sends only traffic from them into the tunnel, and has
no DNS line.

addresses.description: The tunnel's addresses as /32s (the wg-quick `Address`); empty until the subscription is active.

allowed_ips.description:
The `AllowedIPs` of our side on your router: 0.0.0.0/0, so traffic
from anyone to your static addresses comes through the tunnel and
your replies go back. Don't let your router route its whole
connection there: route only traffic from your static addresses
into the tunnel (the dashboard's file does it on Linux).

server_pubkey.description: The exit's WireGuard public key (base64); null until the exit has reported it.

TunnelCredentials.description: Shown once; we can't show them again (make new ones instead).

addresses.description: The addresses routed down this tunnel, as /32s.

allowance_bytes.description:
The account's data this month, pooled across its tunnels (every
tunnel's plan's, plus monthly data and add-ons, which are the
account's): the same on every tunnel. Past it, every tunnel is
slowed to its plan's slowed speed.

peak_mbps.description: The speed ceiling in effect (the plan's or its peak tier's).

`pending_payment`, `setup_required` (a WireGuard tunnel without a
key yet), `active`, `suspended`, `canceled`.

used_bytes.description: This tunnel's share of the account's month, both directions.

pubkey.description: The client's WireGuard public key, base64 of 32 bytes (not all zeros nor of low order, not a server's key). Never the private key.

What the router's configuration needs besides the tunnel's own
fields (never a secret). WireGuard: `wireguard` (as
`TunnelConfig`). L2TP/IPsec: `server` (the user name, the IPsec
identity and IKE version are the tunnel's `l2tp_username`,
`ipsec_id`, `ike`; `ipsec_server_id` is ours) and `mtu`.

ipsec_server_id.description: Our IKE identity (l2tp_ipsec), the router's "remote ID".

server.description: The host name your router connects to.

TunnelStatus.description: The tunnel's live state, as the exit last reported it.

rate_bps_rx.description: Bits per second to you, over the last report.

up.description: A handshake within the last 3 minutes.

updated_at.description: When the exit last reported (null before the first report).

TunnelType.description:
`wireguard` (encrypted; works behind any NAT) or `l2tp_ipsec`
(encrypted; IKEv2 works behind any NAT, IKEv1 needs a fixed public
address). Both are encrypted.

endpoint.description: Your fixed public IPv4 (l2tp_ipsec with ikev1).

pubkey.description: WireGuard's public key (optional: set it later with `PUT /v1/tunnels/{id}/key`).

days.description: One entry per UTC day with traffic, oldest first.

bearer.description:
API token (`opwan_...`), created in the dashboard (Settings → API
tokens). An operation that allows tokens lists the scope it needs
(`bearer: [read]` or `bearer: [write]`); a `write` token also has
`read`.

x-opwan-scopes.read: Read the account, the tunnel's configuration, the firewalls and usage.
x-opwan-scopes.write: Everything read allows, and replace the tunnel's key and the firewalls.

session.description: Session cookie set by the sign-in callback (`opwan_session` on a plain-HTTP dev server).
session.name: __Host-opwan_session

info.description:
The dashboard (`web/`) is the main client; scripts use API tokens. This
document is published at `GET /v1/openapi.json` (without the Stripe
webhook). The source of truth for every
route of `opwan-cp` (docs/design.md, "Control plane API"):
`internal/cp/api/operations_gen.go` is generated from this file and a test
fails when a handler exists for an operation that is not here, or the
other way round.

Authentication: a session cookie (`__Host-opwan_session`; `opwan_session`
on a plain-HTTP dev server, where the `__Host-` prefix is impossible), set
by the sign-in callback after "Sign in with your op account" at opauth
(OIDC code flow with PKCE). Writes carried by the cookie are refused with
403 `csrf_rejected` unless their `Origin` is the dashboard's.

API tokens: created in the dashboard (Settings → API tokens), sent as
`Authorization: Bearer opwan_...` (the `bearer` scheme). A token has one
scope: `read` (the GET operations that allow tokens) or `write` (those
and the writes that allow tokens: the tunnel's key and the firewall).
An operation whose `security` names `bearer` allows tokens, with the
scope it lists; any other signed-in operation is session only (403
`session_required` for a token): checkout, subscription changes,
`/v1/billing/*`, sign-out and the token management itself. A `read`
token on a write is 403 `insufficient_scope`. An unknown, revoked or
expired token is 401 `unauthenticated`. A request with a token never
needs an `Origin`. Each token has its own rate limit (429
`rate_limited`).

Rate limits (per client network, and per account once signed in) answer
429 `rate_limited` with `Retry-After`; the dashboard's normal use stays
far below them.

Errors are RFC 9457 problem documents (`application/problem+json`) with a
stable machine `code`, a plain-language `detail` (what happened, whether it
is you or us, what to do next), `errors[]` for validation problems (422
`validation_failed`), and `request_id`, the reference our logs carry (also
in the `X-Request-Id` header of every response).

Units: bytes are counted in both directions through the exit (rx = to
you, tx = from you); a TB is 10^12 bytes. Speeds are in Mbps (plans) and
bits per second (live rates). Months are calendar months in UTC
(`YYYY-MM`): the data allowance resets on the 1st.
info.summary: The control plane API of opwan, a static public IPv4 address over WireGuard.
info.title: opwan API

get.description:
Every address of the account (the account owns them: one per
tunnel plus its extra addresses), lowest first, with where each goes
(a tunnel, BGP, or unassigned), and how many the account pays for.

entitlement.description: How many addresses the account pays for (one per tunnel plus the extra addresses).

200.description: The addresses, lowest first, and the entitlement.

get.summary: The account's addresses and where each is assigned.

post.description:
Buys a contiguous, size-aligned block of 1, 2, 4 or 8 addresses
(/32 to /29) at the account's location, routed whole down one
tunnel (`tunnel`), or kept unassigned (`kind: unassigned`, the
default). Every address of the block is usable. Each is an extra
address ($3 a month, from `GET /v1/plans`), prorated and charged at
once; a refused card keeps nothing (402). No cap but the location's
free space: 409 `location_full` when it has no free aligned block of
that size (nothing charged).
post.summary: Buy addresses, as one block (billed at once).

delete.description:
Releases the address, or every address of its block, into the
usual 30-day quarantine, and lowers the extra addresses as many
(credited, prorated). 409 `below_included`: each tunnel includes
one address the account keeps.
delete.summary: Give up an address, or the whole block it belongs to.

put.description:
Instant and free: the address stays the account's (no release, no
quarantine) and its firewall rules follow it. An address bought in a
block moves with its whole block (`Address.block`). `{"tunnel": id}`
routes it down that tunnel; `{"kind": "unassigned"}` keeps it
without routing it (traffic to it is dropped); `{"kind": "bgp"}`
makes it float: it goes to whichever of the account's BGP tunnels
announces it, and is dropped while none does (409
`bgp_unavailable` until the account has a tunnel with BGP on at
the address's location).
put.summary: Route an address down a tunnel, to BGP, or nowhere.

get.description:
The default inbound policy and the ordered rules of one of your
addresses (first match wins). TCP port 25 is always blocked in both
directions, whatever the rules say. A new address allows everything
inbound (except TCP 25). 404 `not_found` for an address that is not
yours.

parameters.description: One of the account's addresses (dotted IPv4).
parameters.name: ip

put.description:
Replaces the default policy and every rule at once; applied at the
exit within seconds. At most 64 rules. `ports` (ports and ranges
separated by commas, "80, 443, 8000-8100", 1 to 65535, at most 32 per
rule) only with `tcp` or `udp`, null for every port; stored
normalised (sorted, duplicates dropped, overlapping ranges merged).
`source` an IPv4 address or CIDR, null for anywhere. A TCP rule
naming port 25 (alone or inside a range) is refused: port 25 is
always blocked, so split the range around it (1-24, 26-…). 422
`validation_failed` with `errors[]` fields like `rules[2].ports`.

post.description:
Ends the session (the cookie is cleared) and returns opauth's
end-session URL, where the dashboard sends the browser to end the op
account's sign-in too. Signing out without a session is not an error.

redirect_url.description: opauth's end-session URL (or the dashboard when opauth names none).

get.description:
Checks the state, exchanges the code (private_key_jwt client
assertion), verifies the ID token, creates the opwan account on the
first sign-in (keyed by the op account's `sub`), sets the session
cookie and redirects to the dashboard at `return_to`. A refusal
redirects to the dashboard's `/?auth_error=<code>` with, when we
logged the cause, `&ref=<request id>`. Codes: `oidc_failed` (the
sign-in could not be completed), `access_denied` (you declined at
opauth), `account_closed`.

302.description: Redirect to the dashboard (signed in), or to `/?auth_error=<code>[&ref=<request id>]`.

get.summary: opauth's redirect back after the sign-in.

get.description:
Redirects the browser to opauth's authorization endpoint (code flow,
PKCE S256, state and nonce kept in a sealed, HttpOnly, ten-minute
cookie). A top-level navigation, never a fetch. `return_to` is a
dashboard path (or a URL on the dashboard's origin) to land on after;
anything else is ignored. 503 `oidc_unavailable` when opauth can't be
reached.

parameters.description: Dashboard path or URL on the dashboard origin to return to.
parameters.name: return_to

parameters.description: `login` asks opauth for a fresh sign-in.
parameters.name: prompt

get.summary: Sign in with your op account.

post.description:
Returns the URL of a one-time Stripe Checkout for `tb` terabytes
(1 to 20) added to this calendar month's allowance once paid. A
slowed tunnel gets its full speed back within a minute of the
payment. 409 `no_subscription` without an active subscription.
post.summary: Buy extra data for this month (Stripe Checkout, one-time).

post.description:
Returns the URL of a Stripe customer portal session: payment method,
billing address and tax id, invoices, and cancellation at the
period's end (plan and extra addresses: `PUT /v1/subscription`). 409
`no_subscription` before the first checkout.

Returns the URL of a Stripe Checkout session for a plan and 0 to 2
extra addresses; the dashboard sends the browser there. `location`
(optional) records the location chosen in the location step: the
addresses are assigned there as soon as Stripe confirms the payment
(webhook), before any tunnel exists, and the tunnel must then be
created at that location. An unknown location is 422; one not taking
new customers (no free address) 409 `location_unavailable`; a
different one while addresses or a tunnel exist elsewhere 409
`location_locked`. 409
`already_subscribed` when the account has a live subscription (change
it with `PUT /v1/subscription`), 503 `billing_unavailable` when billing is off or
Stripe can't be reached. `accept_terms_version` must be the terms of
service version in effect (`GET /v1/meta`, `terms_version`): the
customer accepted them by continuing; the acceptance is recorded with
its time. Another or no version: 422 on `accept_terms_version`.

delete.description:
Your addresses are unlinked from the opdns profile (at once when opdns
answers, else we keep trying: `linked_ips` shows what is still
linked). Your tunnel's configuration doesn't change.

get.description:
opdns DNS: with it on, opwan links your static addresses to the opdns
profile you picked, so lookups that reach opdns's resolver (`resolver`,
23.166.164.53) from them are filtered by it. opwan's configurations
never set DNS (opwan isn't a VPN: only your static addresses' traffic
uses the tunnel): point a device or server that uses a static address
at `resolver` for its lookups. Offered when your op account also has an opdns
account (`opdns_account`; null when opdns couldn't be asked just now):
`profiles` are your opdns profiles. `state` is `off`, `pending` (opdns
not updated yet; we keep trying), `linked` or `error` (`error` says what
happened in plain words); `linked_ips` are the addresses opdns has
linked now (addresses released or quarantined are unlinked within a
minute). `available` is false when this server doesn't offer it.
get.summary: The opdns DNS opt-in, and the opdns profiles to pick from.

put.description:
`profile_id` must be one of the `profiles` `GET /v1/dns` lists (422
otherwise; opdns checks again that it is yours). 409
`no_opdns_account` when your op account has no opdns account; 503
`opdns_unavailable` when opdns couldn't be asked (nothing changed).
Your addresses are linked at once when opdns answers, else `state` is
`pending` and we keep trying. Your tunnel's configuration doesn't
change: it has no DNS line either way.
put.summary: Turn opdns DNS on with one of your opdns profiles, or change the profile.

post.description:
One answer of the register-interest form on https://opwan.io (the
next locations people want, and how they'd use opwan), kept until
its email address is confirmed (double opt-in). No sign-in; CORS for
the site's origin only (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin:
https://opwan.io`, never with credentials), and a request from any
other page's `Origin` is 403 `origin_refused`. `Content-Type:
application/json` only (415), at most 8 KiB (413).

In order: the honeypot (a filled `website` gets `sent` and nothing
is kept); the answers' checks (422 `validation_failed`, one entry
of `errors[]` per answer to change, with the form's own message);
the Cloudflare Turnstile token (403 `verification_failed`; 503
`verification_unavailable` when Turnstile doesn't answer); then
`state`:
  - `updated`: the address is already confirmed; its answers are
    replaced, no email.
  - `sent`: the answers are kept as pending and a confirmation link
    (`https://opwan.io/confirm/?t=...`, 48 hours, single use) is
    emailed.
  - `recent`: the address got a link less than 10 minutes ago, or 5
    in 24 hours; its answers are replaced and the earlier link
    still works.
429 `rate_limited`: 10 requests a minute per network, or 10
confirmation emails an hour to one network (`Retry-After: 3600`).
502 `email_failed`: the confirmation email couldn't be sent. 503
`interest_unavailable`: the form is not set up on this deployment.
The raw IP address is never kept, only a salted one-way hash.

post.description:
Called by the site's `/confirm/` page with the token of the emailed
link (never by the link itself, so a mail scanner that follows
links confirms nothing). The token works once and for 48 hours;
the answer then counts. Links emailed before the form moved here
keep working. No sign-in; the same CORS, origin and body rules as
`POST /v1/interest` (at most 1 KiB). 400 `link_incomplete` (not a
token), 404 `link_invalid` (unknown, used, or its answer deleted),
410 `link_expired`.

get.description:
The enabled locations (v1 Dallas only) with what the location step
shows: city and country, the location's network capacity in Gbps,
its ping-test address (answers ICMP echo from anywhere, so you can
measure your latency before buying), whether it has a free
address now, and its maintenance window in progress or next
(`maintenance`). Never lists or counts servers. No sign-in;
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (no credentials), so the site
(https://opwan.io) can show a location under maintenance.
get.summary: The exit locations, for the location step.

get.description:
The signed-in account, its subscription (null before the first
checkout), its first tunnel (`tunnel`: null before one is created, or
when the first tunnel isn't WireGuard), every tunnel (`tunnels`),
its addresses and where each goes, and this month's usage (the
account's, pooled across its tunnels). 401 `unauthenticated` when
signed out.
get.summary: The account and everything it has.

get.description: The running version of the control plane and the API document's version. No sign-in.

The customer API's OpenAPI document as JSON, generated from
`api/openapi.yaml` when the control plane is built: every operation
but the Stripe webhook. Cacheable (`Cache-Control: public`, an
`ETag`; `If-None-Match` answers 304). No sign-in;
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.

The catalogue, from the single source of plans (`internal/plans`), so
the dashboard never hard-codes a price. Prices are USD cents per month,
tax exclusive; the data add-on is one-time, for the current month.
No sign-in.
get.summary: The plans and add-ons on sale.

put.description:
Changes the live subscription at once: what costs more is prorated
and invoiced immediately to the saved card. New addresses are
assigned within seconds; removed ones (the highest first) stop
routing at once and are quarantined. More `monthly_tb` adds to
the allowance at once; less is not credited: the allowance keeps
the most of the billing period (`monthly_tb_counted`) and the new
amount renews from the next period (going back up to what the
period counts costs nothing more). An absent `monthly_tb` keeps
the current amount. `peak_mbps` changes the peak speed tier at
once, prorated (Plus only; 1000 is Plus's own ceiling, no tier); an
absent `peak_mbps` keeps the current tier on Plus, and changing to
Base removes it (Base's ceiling is 500 Mbps). Stripe's customer portal can't
change a subscription with several items, hence this route. 409
`no_subscription` without a live subscription, 402
`payment_failed` when the card is refused (nothing changes).
put.summary: Change the plan, the extra addresses, the monthly data or the peak speed.

get.description:
Every API token of the account, oldest first: name, scope, when it
was made, last used (refreshed at most once a minute) and when it
expires. Never the token itself. Session cookie only: a token gets
403 `session_required`.

post.description:
Creates an API token with a name (1 to 100 characters), a scope
(`read` or `write`) and an optional expiry in the future. The token
(`opwan_` and 52 base32 characters) is in this answer only: we keep
its SHA-256. At most 20 tokens per account (409 `too_many_tokens`:
revoke one first). Session cookie only: a token gets 403
`session_required`.

delete.description:
Revokes one of the account's API tokens at once: its next request
is 401 `unauthenticated`. 404 `not_found` for a token that is not
the account's. Session cookie only: a token gets 403
`session_required`.

put.description:
Creates the account's one tunnel at a location, or replaces its
WireGuard public key (re-keying: the old key's peer goes, the new
one is live at the next desired state; the location can't change
once created, and must be the one chosen at checkout when one was:
409 `location_locked` otherwise). Send only the **public** key:
the private key is generated in the browser, or by the customer on
their own device (bring your own key), and never reaches us. 422 on
`pubkey` when it isn't base64 of exactly 32 bytes, is all zeros or
another point of low order, or is one of our servers' keys. Addresses are assigned while the subscription is
active (1 + extra IPs); before that the tunnel is `pending_payment`
and `config.addresses` is empty. The answer is everything the client
configuration needs besides the private key. 409 `pubkey_in_use`
when another tunnel has that key.
put.summary: Create the tunnel, or replace its key.

get.description:
The same data as `PUT /v1/tunnel`'s `config`: endpoint, server public
key, addresses and the suggested client settings. Never a private
key. `server_pubkey` is null until the exit server has reported its
key (seconds after the first start). 404 `not_found` without a
tunnel.

Every tunnel of the account, by number (docs/tunnels.md): each one is
a billing line with its own plan, type, allowance, usage, status and
client configuration. Never a secret.

max_tunnels.description: How many tunnels an account may have.

post.description:
Adds a tunnel to the live subscription: its plan's price (and its
peak tier) is prorated and charged to the saved card at once; a
refused card creates nothing (402). The tunnel gets one new address
of the account's location, assigned to it, and its plan's data joins
the account's pool. The account's first tunnel (paid at checkout,
none made yet) is made on the subscription's own line, without a
charge (`plan` and `peak_mbps` are then ignored). For
L2TP/IPsec the answer carries `credentials`, **shown this once**.
409 `no_subscription` (subscribe first: the first tunnel is bought
through checkout), `tunnel_limit`, `location_full` (nothing was
charged), `type_unavailable`, `endpoint_in_use`, `pubkey_in_use`.

201.description: The new tunnel, with its credentials for L2TP/IPsec.

delete.description:
Removes the tunnel and its billing line (the rest of the period is
credited, as Stripe prorates). Extra addresses above 2 per remaining
tunnel are lowered to that (credited too). The tunnel's addresses
stay the account's, unassigned, as long as the account's
entitlement (one per tunnel plus the extra addresses) covers them;
otherwise `release` names the ones to give up (the usual 30-day
quarantine), and without it the most recently added go, a block
always whole (single addresses are not preferred: newest first). 409
`release_required` (with `release_count`) when `release` names too
few. 409 `last_tunnel` (cancel the
subscription in Billing instead).

get.description:
One of the account's tunnels, as in `GET /v1/tunnels` (never a
secret). 404 `not_found` for another account's tunnel.

patch.description:
Sets the tunnel's name (1 to 40 characters, one line), shown in the
dashboard only. 422 on `name`.

get.description:
Customer BGP over the tunnel (free, off by default): its settings,
our side's values, the session's state, and the routes received,
accepted and refused (with the reason). `available` says whether
the tunnel's location offers BGP; `full_table_available` whether
it can send the full table.

refused.reason: Only single addresses (/32) of your account are accepted.

get.summary: The tunnel's BGP session and what it announces.

put.description:
`enabled` true takes `export` (`default`, the default; or `full`)
and `auth` (`none`, `md5` or `ao`: TCP-AO is recommended; we make
the key). Turning it on gives the tunnel its session addresses,
kept while the tunnel exists, and, the first time for the account,
the account its AS number: a private 32-bit number we choose
(`asn` in the reply), unique to the account and the same for all
its tunnels' sessions. You don't choose it: a request with `asn` is
refused (422 on `asn`). 503 `asn_unavailable`: no number could be
given just now (BGP stays off; try again).
Turning it off ends the session; addresses assigned to BGP stay
assigned and are dropped while none of the account's tunnels
announces them. 409 `bgp_unavailable` (the location doesn't offer
BGP yet), 409 `full_table_unavailable`, 409 `full_table_full`.

refused.reason: Only single addresses (/32) of your account are accepted.

put.summary: Turn BGP on or off for the tunnel, or change its settings.

get.description:
Our AS number and address, yours, the key if the session has one,
the addresses the session may announce, and configuration examples
for BIRD, FRR (and UniFi gateways), MikroTik RouterOS 7, Ubiquiti
EdgeOS and OpenWrt. It holds the key: a session or a write token.
409 `bgp_off` while BGP is off for the tunnel.

examples.config: protocol bgp opwan { local 169.254.64.3 as 4200000001; neighbor 169.254.64.2 as 403104; ttl security yes; ... }
examples.title: BIRD 2

get.summary: The session's values to paste into your router, with examples.

post.description:
A new TCP-MD5 password or TCP-AO key for a session with
authentication; the old one stops at the next desired state
(seconds), so the session restarts once your router has the new
one. 409 `bgp_no_auth` when the session has none.

examples.config: protocol bgp opwan { local 169.254.64.3 as 4200000001; neighbor 169.254.64.2 as 403104; ttl security yes; ... }
examples.title: BIRD 2

200.description: The session's values to paste, with the new key.

post.summary: A new key for the tunnel's BGP session.

post.description:
A new IPsec pre-shared key and L2TP password; the old ones stop
working at the next desired state (seconds). 409 `not_l2tp` for a
WireGuard tunnel.

200.description: The tunnel and its new credentials.

post.summary: New credentials for an L2TP/IPsec tunnel (shown once).

put.description:
As `PUT /v1/tunnel` (re-keying, bring your own key) for any
WireGuard tunnel. 409 `not_wireguard` for the other types.
put.summary: Set or replace a WireGuard tunnel's public key.

put.description:
This tunnel's plan and peak tier, prorated and charged (or
credited) at once. Monthly data and extra addresses are the
account's: `PUT /v1/subscription`. An absent `peak_mbps` keeps the
current one.
put.summary: Change a tunnel's plan, monthly data or peak speed.

put.description:
Sets the tunnel's type and what that type needs: a WireGuard public
key; for L2TP/IPsec `ike` (`ikev2`, or `ikev1` with your fixed
public IPv4 in `endpoint`). The price doesn't change. The old setup
stops at the next desired state. L2TP/IPsec gets new
`credentials`, shown this once. 409
`type_unavailable`, `endpoint_in_use`, `pubkey_in_use`.

200.description: The tunnel, with credentials for L2TP/IPsec.

put.summary: Change a tunnel's type (and its setup).

get.description:
Totals and the daily series (UTC days) of a calendar month (default
the current one), the month's allowance (plan plus data add-ons) and
the tunnel's live state (`live`, null without a tunnel). Months before
the account existed answer zeros.
get.summary: Data used in a month, per day, and live throughput.
